explanations: terra: People were lifeless, God gave them life, will cause them to die and give them life again, then they return to Him; the full movement belongs to God.
terra: They will never wish for death because of what their hands sent ahead; prior deeds shape even what a person dares to wish at the threshold of return.
terra: Whatever good people send ahead لِأَنفُسِكُم is found with God, making the section's “for my life” a present command with a promised destination.

luna: The section distinguishes bodily death from the life that follows; this ayah forbids calling those killed in God's way dead and says they are alive, a direct boundary on what “life” means. | terra: Those killed in God's way must not be called dead but living, though people do not perceive it; apparent bodily death does not exhaust the Qur'anic field of life.
terra: Fear, hunger, and loss are named as tests, giving the living setting in which the patient response of return in 2:156 is formed.
terra: Those who answer calamity with “we belong to God and to Him we return” voice the return while still living, rather than learning its direction only when driven.
terra: Those patient responders receive blessings, mercy, and guidance from their Lord, completing the favorable consequence of consciously belonging and returning.
terra: Followers wish for a return so they could disown their leaders as the leaders disowned them; God shows their deeds as regrets from which they cannot leave the Fire.
terra: Pilgrims are commanded to take provision, then told that the best provision is mindfulness; the journey's literal supplies become a concrete model for moral provision sent toward arrival.
terra: This ayah joins two section words: أَنَّىٰ in the sense “however” and the command وَقَدِّمُوا۟ لِأَنفُسِكُمْ, turning future provision into an instruction addressed to embodied life.

terra: أَنَّىٰ يُحْىِۦ هَٰذِهِ ٱللَّهُ asks how God will revive a ruined town after death, and God demonstrates revival; “how?” opens onto divine life-giving here but closes onto human benefit in 89:23.
terra: Abraham asks to see how God revives the dead so that his heart may be reassured; tranquility here grows through witnessed resurrection rather than through denial of it.
terra: A Day of return to God is feared, when every soul is paid fully for what it earned; return and individual recompense meet directly.
terra: When people are gathered for the certain Day, every soul is paid fully for what it earned, specifying the individual settlement of the record.

luna: The section's delayed wish to have sent good forward is reflected in each soul finding its deeds present; its wish for a far distance from its evil makes the regret sharper. | terra: Every soul finds its good and evil deeds present and wishes a vast distance from the evil; what was done has arrived before it, and wishing cannot remove it.
terra: Zechariah asks Mary أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا about the source of her provision, illustrating the source section's “from where?” sense of the same word.
terra: Zechariah asks أَنَّىٰ he can have a son in old age with a barren wife; “how?” frames life that appears humanly unavailable but remains possible to God.
terra: Mary asks أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى وَلَدٌ, “how can I have a child?”, and the answer asserts God's creative command; an apparently closed “how” here opens into new life by divine power.
terra: God makes promised help good news so that hearts may be reassured by it; the settled condition is rooted in trust that comes before the final meeting.
terra: When believers wrong themselves they remember God, seek forgiveness, and do not knowingly persist; remembrance still repairs action here because it comes before judgment.

luna: The section's life reaches beyond death; this ayah says those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord and provided for, specifying a continuing life beyond bodily death. | terra: Those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord and provided for, locating life and provision beyond the worldly ending.
terra: Punishment is said to be بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ, so what the hands advanced becomes the ground of the later encounter rather than disappearing into the past.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for root ح ي ي includes the afterlife, and its prose calls that the true life; this ayah contrasts every soul tasting death with receiving its full reward on the Resurrection Day. | terra: Every soul tastes death, receives full reward at resurrection, and learns that worldly life was deceptive enjoyment; soul, death, reckoning, and the lesser life meet in one ayah.
terra: Repentance is not for the person who persists until death arrives and then says “I repent now”; the ayah marks the temporal boundary of useful recollection.
terra: When disaster strikes because of what their hands sent ahead, they come swearing good intentions; consequence produces a belated reinterpretation of their acts.
terra: Worldly enjoyment is little and the Hereafter better for the mindful; the comparison directs present restraint toward the longer life.
terra: Angels take those who wronged their souls and question their excuse before Hell becomes their refuge; this interrogated taking reverses the tranquil soul's unforced welcome.
terra: The text condemns what their souls قَدَّمَتْ لَهُمْ: divine anger and lasting punishment; a soul can send ruin ahead as concretely as it can send good.
terra: The disciples say the heavenly table would reassure their hearts and let them know the truth, showing reassurance sought through a confirming sign.
terra: On the Day truthfulness benefits the truthful, eternal Gardens culminate in God being pleased with them and they with Him; mutual approval supplies the horizon of the pleased soul.

luna: The section's “if only” comes after the decisive event; here people facing the Fire wish to be returned so they would not deny God's signs, a matching late plea. | terra: Standing over the Fire, they wish to be returned so they could stop denying the signs and become believers; visible punishment triggers an unusable resolve.

luna: The section's regret cannot undo what preceded it; this next ayah says that even if the deniers were returned, they would repeat what they had been forbidden to do, exposing the wish as no real remedy. | terra: What they concealed has appeared, yet a return would lead them back to the same prohibition; it denies that a spoken late wish proves a changed soul.
terra: The deniers say there is only worldly life and no resurrection, stating exactly the mistaken location of life that the later judgment scene overturns.
terra: When made to stand before their Lord they admit the resurrection is true and are told to taste punishment for denial; certainty arrives at the closed moment.

luna: The section's human recognizes too late what should have been done; this ayah says that when the Hour comes suddenly, people lament what they neglected, matching the same sudden arrival and regret.
terra: Worldly life is play and diversion while the Hereafter is better for the mindful; it distinguishes the life lived as distraction from the life worth preparing for.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for root ن ف س concerns the living soul, and it describes souls taken in sleep and death; this ayah says God takes people at night and raises them again by day, adding the recurring sleep-and-return scene. | terra: God takes people by night, knows what they acquired by day, and raises them again until the fixed term; each waking is a temporary return before the final one.
terra: At the arrival of death God's messengers take the person without neglect, identifying the agents and exactness of the soul's departure.
terra: They are then returned to God, their true Master, whose judgment is decisive; the taking in the preceding ayah has a stated destination.
terra: A soul can be held for what it earned, and no ransom or intercession can release it; acquisition in this life determines its later captivity.

luna: The section contrasts a soul invited to return with souls forcibly extracted at death; this ayah's أَخْرِجُوا أَنْفُسَكُمُ and humiliating punishment stage the opposite encounter. | terra: At death the angels stretch out their hands and command wrongdoers أَخْرِجُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمُ, followed by humiliating punishment; forced extraction is the sharp opposite of the tranquil soul being invited to return.
terra: People come to God individually as first created and leave granted possessions behind; what was treated as “my life” cannot accompany the returning soul.
terra: God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, then asks أَنَّىٰ people are turned away; the section's “how?” word is joined directly to life's boundary.

luna: The section contrasts a still-open time for remembrance with recollection at the arrival of the end; this ayah sets a boundary: faith then will not benefit a soul that had not believed before. | terra: When certain signs of the Lord arrive, new belief or belief that had earned no good no longer benefits a soul; the ayah explicitly marks the boundary of useful faith.
terra: Each soul earns only against itself, no bearer carries another's burden, and all return to their Lord to be informed; earning, individuality, and return converge.
terra: When the messengers take the wrongdoers' souls, they ask where the invoked partners are, and the dying admit those partners have vanished.
terra: Garden dwellers are told that they inherited the Garden for what they used to do, making entry the arrived result of prior action.
terra: Those deceived by worldly life forgot the meeting of their Day, so they are forgotten then; their treatment of remembrance becomes their judgment condition.

luna: The section's image is recollection after the decisive event; here those who forgot the revelation say the messengers brought truth only when its fulfillment arrives, then ask whether they can return. | terra: When the promised outcome arrives, rejecters admit the messengers told the truth and ask for intercession or a return to act differently; their selves are already lost.
terra: When a satanic impulse touches the mindful, they remember and immediately see clearly; this is timely recollection that changes the present state.
terra: The parallel promise of angelic help is made so hearts may be reassured, another concrete use of the state named by ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ.
terra: Believers are commanded to answer God and the Messenger when called to what gives them life, placing life in a responsive act that must occur before the final gathering.

luna: The section contrasts its tranquil soul with a forced departure; this ayah depicts angels taking the disbelievers' souls while striking their faces and backs, another specific opposite death scene. | terra: Angels take the unbelievers while striking faces and backs and ordering them to taste burning; this violent taking opposes the call to the settled soul.
terra: The same formula, بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيكُمْ, is spoken in the death scene where angels strike the unbelievers, joining prior deeds to their immediate recompense.
terra: Believers are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter, whose scale makes worldly enjoyment little.
terra: The foremost believers receive God's pleasure, their pleasure in Him, and eternal Gardens; the satisfied state is joined to a life of prior faithful action.
terra: Believers are promised قَدَمَ صِدْقٍ with their Lord, a true prior standing that closely matches the dictionary source's “preceding قدم” and enduring good already with God.
terra: Those who are content with and reassured by worldly life while heedless of the signs attach tranquility to the wrong life, reversing the settled soul's readiness for return.
terra: God originates creation and repeats it, followed by فَأَنَّىٰ تُؤْفَكُونَ; the same question-word challenges refusal of renewed life.
luna: The section links the arrival of punishment with belated remembrance; this ayah says those who did wrong conceal regret when they see the punishment, tying the vision of the outcome to remorse.

luna: The section shows recognition after the crisis has arrived; Pharaoh says آمنت while drowning, a direct scene of belief voiced at the point when rescue is too late. | terra: At drowning Pharaoh declares belief in Israel's God, offering a historical scene of certainty and confession arriving with destruction.

luna: The section's late remembrance is answered by this rebuke to Pharaoh: آالآن, “now?”, marks the boundary between a timely response and one made after disobedience is complete. | terra: “Now?” answers that confession by recalling his earlier rebellion and corruption, denying the saving force of recognition at the closed moment.
terra: Pharaoh goes ahead of his people on resurrection day and leads them into the Fire; this ruinous human “advance” reverses sending good ahead to God.

luna: The section explicitly contrasts its tranquil soul with the soul described here; this ayah calls the النفس prone to commanding evil except where the Lord shows mercy. | terra: The soul that relentlessly commands evil is an opposing state to the soul whose turmoil has settled and which can return well pleased.
terra: The righteous enter perpetual Gardens with their righteous kin, giving the communal Garden entry promised after the individual soul's return.
terra: Angels enter through every gate saying “Peace upon you for your patience,” making prior endurance the reason for the peaceful reception.
terra: People rejoice in worldly life even though it is only a small enjoyment compared with the Hereafter, exposing joy attached to what passes.

luna: The section's final النفس المطْمَئِنَّة is a soul at rest; this ayah says hearts find rest in God's remembrance, giving a specific Qur'anic relation between remembrance and inward calm. | terra: Believing hearts become tranquil بِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ; this joins timely remembrance to the settled state embodied by ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ.
terra: Those who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter also obstruct God's way, so the misplaced preference becomes a course of action rather than a mere opinion.
terra: Death comes to the punished person from every direction, yet he does not die; this grotesque suspension clarifies the section's richer use of “my life.”

luna: The section portrays a wish for more time after the final event; this warning says wrongdoers will ask their Lord for a short delay so they can respond and follow the messengers, a concrete version of that impossible postponement. | terra: Those facing punishment ask for a brief respite so they can answer the call and follow the messengers; even a little returned time is now unavailable.
terra: God repays every soul for what it earned, the final destination of action performed in the preceding life.
terra: The unbelievers will come to wish that they had been Muslims; the future wish states the same late recognition without yet staging all its consequences.
terra: Eating, enjoyment, and distracting hopes occupy them until they come to know, identifying the nearer life that postpones the recognition predicted just before.
terra: No community can advance or delay its fixed term, supplying the temporal limit beneath the unbelievers' later wish in 15:2.
terra: Once the human is fashioned and God breathes into him of His spirit, the angels are commanded to prostrate; breathed spirit marks the completion of embodied human life.
terra: “Enter it in peace, secure” is a direct Garden welcome that parallels the tranquil soul's commanded entry.

luna: The section's settled soul is spoken to gently, unlike a soul taken under force; this ayah describes angels taking people who wronged themselves as they offer submission at death. | terra: Angels take those who wronged their souls; their late submission and denial of wrongdoing receive rebuttal, unlike the good soul's truthful, peaceful reception.

luna: The section's tranquil soul is addressed with a return and welcome; here angels take the good in a good state, greet them with peace, and tell them to enter the Garden. | terra: Angels take the good while saying “Peace upon you; enter the Garden for what you did,” combining a gentle taking of souls with peaceful entry earned by prior action.
terra: When wrongdoers see the punishment it is neither lightened nor delayed, so recognition at sight creates no new interval for action.
terra: What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, stating the passing-versus-lasting measure behind sending provision ahead.
terra: A believing doer of righteousness is promised a good life and later reward according to the best deeds, joining lived action to both present and future life.
terra: A heart can remain مُطْمَئِنٌّۢ بِٱلْإِيمَٰنِ even under coercion, locating tranquility in durable faith rather than outward ease.
terra: Disbelief after faith is explained by preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, showing how the chosen “life” forms the soul before return.
terra: Every soul comes pleading for itself and is paid fully for what it did, showing the soul speaking only after its deeds have become fixed evidence.

terra: A town was secure and tranquil with abundant provision, then ingratitude turned its state into hunger and fear; outward ease is shown to be a reversible tranquility unlike the faithful soul's settledness.

luna: The section's wish concerns what a person sent ahead for their life; this ayah says each person's record will be brought out on the Resurrection Day, making the life review an individual record. | terra: Each person's deed-record is fastened to his neck and brought out as an opened book at resurrection; the past accompanies the person bodily into judgment.

luna: After the record is brought out in 17:13, this ayah tells each person to read their book and serve as their own reckoner, a direct image of confronting what one has done. | terra: “Read your book; your own soul is sufficient as reckoner today” makes self-knowledge unavoidable once the time for changing the record is gone.
terra: Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as it deserves while believing has a striving that is appreciated; this is deliberate preparation for that life.
terra: The ruined garden owner wrings his hands and wishes he had not associated anyone with his Lord; this worldly loss still dramatizes regret before the final judgment scene.
terra: Worldly life is rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry debris scattered by winds, a scene of growth and breath-like dispersal that measures its passing span.
terra: Wealth and children adorn worldly life, but enduring good deeds are better with the Lord for reward and hope; deeds are the portion that can be sent beyond it.

luna: The section imagines looking back at what was sent ahead; here the record is laid open and people find ما عملوا حاضرا, their deeds present before them, giving that review its record-book scene. | terra: The record is laid open, the guilty fear its contents, and all they did is found present; nothing from the lived past is too small to arrive.
terra: The person reminded of God's signs turns away and forgets مَا قَدَّمَتْ يَدَاهُ; it joins refused remembrance to the deeds later recovered too late.
terra: Whoever hopes to meet the Lord is told to do righteous work and avoid associating anyone in worship; expected meeting becomes present preparation.
terra: Zechariah's repeated “how can I have a son?” again places the section's question-word at the boundary between barrenness, age, and divinely given life.
terra: Mary again asks أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى غُلَٰمٌ with no man having touched her; the question concerns the seemingly impossible arrival of life, unlike the impossible recovery of spent moral time.
luna: The section calls 89:23 a remembrance that comes too late; this ayah names Judgment يوم الحسرة, the Day of Regret, while people remain heedless and do not believe.
terra: Enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and return, repeating the distinction between what passes and what reaches its destination.
terra: The coming Hour is kept hidden so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for; the concealed deadline makes present striving meaningful.
terra: The criminal in Hell neither dies nor lives, a negative limit-case that separates mere continued existence from the “life” for which one should prepare.
terra: Turning away from God's remembrance yields a constricted life and blind resurrection, directly tying refused remembrance to a damaged worldly life and later exposure.
terra: The resurrected person asks why he has been raised blind although he once saw, voicing the shocked self-reading of judgment.
terra: God answers that signs came and were forgotten, so the person is forgotten that Day; the judgment condition corresponds to the earlier treatment of remembrance.
terra: Every soul tastes death, is tested with bad and good, and is returned to God; embodied life is an examination whose return discloses its result.
terra: Just scales are set for resurrection and even a mustard seed is brought forward, so no soul loses the smallest provision it made.
terra: God breathes of His spirit into the woman who guarded her chastity and makes her and her son a sign; breath imagery accompanies extraordinary human life.
terra: When the true promise draws near, unbelievers stare and admit they were heedless and unjust; unveiled reality forces the remembrance that heedlessness postponed.
terra: The greatest terror does not grieve the righteous, and angels receive them with “this is your promised Day”; peaceful angelic reception closely parallels the address to the tranquil soul.

terra: Human development from a drop through womb and maturity, alongside dead earth revived by rain, is presented as evidence for resurrection; growing, embodied, and restored life meet in one proof.
terra: The sufferer is told the burning punishment is for what his hands sent ahead, repeating the exact moral motion behind 89:24's regret.
terra: A person serving God on an edge feels reassured when good arrives but turns away under trial, losing both lives; conditional ease is the opposite of a soul stabilized through the test.
terra: The chiefs claim there is only worldly life, generations dying and living with no resurrection; the denial gives the direct opposite of “my life” correctly placed beyond death.

luna: The section depicts a person wishing they had sent something ahead; here death arrives and the person asks رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ, trying to return before the resurrection. | terra: At the arrival of death the person pleads رَبِّ ٱرْجِعُونِ; the requested return is the last attempt to recover the time that the section says has passed.

luna: The section itself cites this answer to the dying person's request: let me return to do صالح work; كَلَّا and the intervening barrier make the missed chance final. | terra: He asks to return and do righteousness in what he left, but كَلَّا closes the request and the barrier remains until resurrection; no deed can now be sent ahead.
terra: The question whether humans thought they were created aimlessly and would not return exposes the false premise behind living without preparation.

luna: The section's speaker wishes they had prepared before the Day; here the wrongdoer bites his hands and says يَا لَيْتَنِي اتَّخَذْتُ مَعَ الرَّسُولِ سَبِيلًا, wishing he had taken a path with the Messenger. | terra: The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger, a bodily image of regret for the route not taken while time was open.

luna: The regret scene in 25:27 continues as a wish not to have taken a particular companion; this adds the specific relationship the wrongdoer blames for the missed path. | terra: He wishes he had not taken a particular person as intimate friend, locating the worldly relation that shaped his lost path.

luna: The section's wording recalls ذ ك ر as remembrance; here the speaker says the companion turned him away from الذكر after it had come, specifying what was lost before the regret. | terra: The friend led him away from the reminder after it had come, connecting the judgment wish to an earlier, received remembrance that was abandoned.
terra: God makes sleep a repose and the day a rising, giving each daily return of consciousness the resurrection pattern that 39:42 locates in taken and released souls.
terra: On the Day when wealth and children do not benefit, ordinary measures of a successful life cannot serve as provision.
terra: Only one who comes to God with a sound heart benefits, offering a close inner parallel to the soul that arrives settled and fit for welcome.
terra: The condemned wish for another turn so they could become believers; the wish names a new identity but cannot supply a new span of action.
terra: The rejecters do not believe until they see the painful punishment, making sight of the consequence the point at which their former refusal finally breaks.
terra: The punishment comes suddenly while they are unaware, closing the interval in which remembrance could still have become action.
terra: Only then do they ask whether they will be granted respite, another request for usable time made after that time has ended.
terra: Whoever brings a good deed receives better than it and is safe from that Day's terror, a prepared deed issuing in inward security.
terra: A messenger is sent lest people blame a calamity on مَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ and ask why no warner came; warning preserves a time for response before regret.
terra: Worldly goods are enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting; it asks the hearer to reason before the comparison becomes visible.
terra: Everything perishes except God's face, judgment belongs to Him, and people return to Him; passing things, enduring sovereignty, and return meet in one boundary.
terra: Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, placing the soul's destination beyond the death that ends its present action.

luna: The section's stated root ح ي ي covers life through the Hereafter; this ayah directly calls the Hereafter الدار الآخرة and says it is الحياة itself, resolving the meaning of “my life.” | terra: The declaration that the Hereafter is لَهِىَ ٱلْحَيَوَانُ identifies it as the real life, explaining why the regretful speaker can finally call that destination “my life.”
terra: People know only the outward aspect of worldly life and are heedless of the Hereafter; knowledge of the surface coexists with forgetfulness of the true destination.
terra: When harm strikes because of what people's hands sent ahead, they despair; the same advance-action idiom operates inside worldly consequence.
terra: The effects of mercy show earth revived after death, and the same God will revive the dead; the growing sense of life points beyond bodily death.

terra: People are warned of a Day when parent and child cannot avail each other and told not to be deceived by worldly life; the true promise demands preparation before kinship and possessions fall away.
terra: No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow or in what land it will die, preserving the hidden deadline that makes advance preparation necessary.
terra: God fashions the human and breathes into him of His spirit before granting hearing, sight, and hearts; breath here marks the body's becoming a living, perceiving person.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for root ن ف س is the life-giving spirit; here the angel of death takes the addressed people and they are returned to their Lord, combining departure and return. | terra: The angel of death takes people fully and then they are returned to their Lord, joining the soul's taking to its ultimate direction.

luna: The section's regret is spoken only after judgment begins; here wrongdoers lower their heads before their Lord and ask to be sent back so they can act righteously, exactly the impossible wish the section describes. | terra: The guilty lower their heads before their Lord and ask to be returned to do righteousness now that they see and hear with certainty.

luna: The section links late recollection to a missed meeting with God; this ayah answers the earlier request to return by naming their having forgotten that day's meeting. | terra: They are told to taste the result of forgetting the meeting of their Day and that they have been forgotten; the missed remembrance becomes irreversible encounter.
terra: Guests are told not to wait for a meal's إِنَىٰهُ, its proper readiness time; the cognate gives the source section's time-root a concrete sense of a moment becoming due.
terra: With faces turned in the Fire, they wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; the lost action becomes clear only inside punishment.
terra: They explain that obedience to leaders and great ones led them from the way, identifying the prior allegiance behind their regret.
terra: They ask for doubled punishment and a great curse on those leaders, showing how late memory assigns blame without reopening action.

luna: The section cites 34:52's failed reach from a distant place; this immediately preceding ayah depicts the terrified people seized from a nearby place with no escape, sharpening the distance and lateness of their grasp.

luna: The section's root ء ن ي appears in وأنى, and its image of reaching after what has passed is sharpened by التناوش من مكان بعيد: the people try to attain faith from a far place when punishment is seen. | terra: After judgment they profess belief, but وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ ٱلتَّنَاوُشُ describes trying to reach it from a far place; this supplies the spatial reach behind the section's backward-stretching hand.
luna: The section uses 34:52 for an unreachable late grasp; this next ayah says they had disbelieved before and had made guesses about the unseen from far away, explaining why that grasp fails.
terra: God's promise is true, so worldly life must not deceive; the warning asks the hearer to relocate confidence before the promised meeting.
terra: Whoever purifies himself does so for his own soul, and the destination is God; self-purification is preparation carried all the way to the return.
terra: Hell's people are neither finished by death nor relieved of punishment, showing an afterlife continuation that is not the desired life.

luna: The section's person wishes too late that they had sent righteous work ahead; here the people in the Fire ask to be brought out to do good differently, and are reminded that they had time to remember and a warner came. | terra: People cry from Hell to be taken out so they can do other than before, but are reminded that they had a sufficient lifespan and a warner.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for root ق د م treats good work as what one sends ahead; this ayah says God records ما قدموا along with their traces, showing that the forwarded work remains recorded. | terra: God records مَا قَدَّمُوا۟ وَءَاثَٰرَهُمْ, preserving both what people send ahead and the traces left behind for the resurrection account.
terra: After being told to enter the Garden, the slain believer wishes his people knew of his forgiveness; this post-death wish seeks their benefit rather than repairing his own missed action.
terra: What he wishes them to know is that his Lord forgave and honored him, completing the generous reversal of the condemned person's self-directed “if only.”
terra: At the trumpet blast people emerge from graves and hasten to their Lord, staging bodily return after the soul's earlier departure.
terra: They cry out about who raised them from their sleeping place, then acknowledge the Merciful's promise and the messengers' truth; awakening brings belated recognition.
terra: The human forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones; forgetfulness of origin produces denial of the later life.
terra: The answer says the One who originated the bones the first time will revive them, replacing forgotten origin with a timely reminder of return.
terra: A Garden speaker asks whether they are then never to die, confronting the permanence of the life reached after the first death.
terra: The speaker specifies that only the first death has occurred and that no punishment follows, marking the Garden's life as secure beyond death.
terra: “This is the great triumph” names that death-surviving outcome as the true success.
terra: “For the like of this let the workers work” turns the unveiled afterlife into a present directive to send effort toward it.
terra: Destroyed generations cried out, but it was no time for escape; the brief formula captures a call made only after the door of response had closed.
terra: The repeated creation formula joins shaping with breathing of spirit, reinforcing breath as the threshold of living personhood.
terra: Revelation makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance, giving remembrance an embodied movement toward settled receptivity.

luna: The section's dictionary entry for root ن ف س identifies the soul as the spirit by which the body lives; this ayah says God takes the souls at death and in sleep, retaining some and releasing others until their term. | terra: God takes the souls at death and those not dead during sleep, retaining one and sending the other back to an appointed term; it stages the section's breath-like departure and permitted return.
terra: People who have transgressed against themselves are told not to despair of divine mercy, opening a present path for the soul before the later regret speech.

luna: The section's late voice discovers too late that it should have prepared; this ayah tells people to turn to their Lord and submit من قبل أن يأتيكم العذاب, while action is still possible. | terra: They are commanded to return to their Lord and submit before punishment comes, the actionable return that prevents an impossible request to return afterward.

luna: The section's recollection comes after the moment to act; this next ayah urges following revelation before punishment arrives suddenly, making explicit the warning that could prevent such regret. | terra: They are told to follow the best revelation before punishment comes suddenly and unnoticed, identifying what must be done before the soul says “alas.”

luna: The section's speaker says “if only I had sent ahead”; this ayah gives another Judgment lament, يا حسرتى على ما فرطت, for having neglected what was owed to God. | terra: A soul cries “Alas for what I neglected concerning God” lest it face punishment; the warning voices the regret now so it need not be spoken too late.

luna: As regret develops after 39:56, this ayah imagines the speaker saying that guidance would have made them among the God-conscious, another late recognition of what was missed. | terra: The same soul imagines saying that, had God guided it, it would have been mindful; this exposes the excuse that follows neglected warning.

luna: The section's wish cannot recover the past; this ayah makes the same wish explicit as لو أن لي كرة, “if only I had another return,” so the speaker could do good. | terra: On seeing punishment it asks for another turn so it can be among the doers of good, exactly the impossible effort to send something ahead after arrival.

luna: The section's remorse follows a warning ignored until too late; this reply says God's signs had already come and were denied, naming the earlier choice behind the regret. | terra: The answer recalls that signs did come but were denied in arrogance; the lost opportunity, not lack of a reminder, caused the late plea.
terra: God saves the mindful in their place of success so evil does not touch them and they do not grieve, an indirect parallel to the tranquil soul's fearless reception.
terra: The trumpet causes all in heavens and earth to fall dead except whom God wills, then a second blast raises them looking on; death and returned awareness are separated only by divine command.
terra: Every soul is paid in full for what it did, binding the soul's final condition to its completed action.
terra: Unbelievers are driven in groups to Hell and questioned by its keepers about the warners; compulsion and accusation reverse the tranquil soul's welcome.
terra: The mindful are conducted in groups to the Garden and greeted with peace by its keepers; this parallels the destination while distinguishing a communal escort from the section's intimate call.
terra: The Garden entrants praise God for fulfilling the promise and letting them settle wherever they wish, voicing contentment after the peaceful welcome of 39:73.
terra: After two deaths and two lives, the condemned confess their sins and ask whether there is any way out; renewed life produces recognition but no new earthly term.
terra: That Day every soul is repaid for what it earned and no injustice occurs, emphasizing immediacy once the judgment moment arrives.
terra: The believer calls worldly life only temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the enduring abode, a direct correction of where lasting life is located.

luna: The section's person remembers only when the final event comes; here people say آمنا بالله وحده when they see punishment, matching the same late turn toward belief. | terra: When they see God's punishment they finally profess faith in God alone and reject former partners, a belief produced by unveiled consequence.

luna: After the people believe on seeing punishment in 40:84, this ayah says their faith does not benefit them then, stating the closed boundary that the section's question implies. | terra: Their faith does not benefit them once they have seen the punishment; this directly states the rule implicit in “how can remembrance benefit him?”

luna: The section's tranquil soul is addressed and welcomed toward the Garden; here angels descend on those who remained steadfast and tell them not to fear or grieve, but to rejoice in the promised Garden. | terra: Angels descend on those steadfast in saying “Our Lord is God” and tell them not to fear or grieve; it closely parallels the calm divine reception of the settled soul.

luna: The angelic welcome in 41:30 continues here with the promise of companionship in this life and the Hereafter and whatever the souls desire, extending the section's welcome to the returning soul. | terra: The angels declare themselves allies in this life and the Hereafter and promise whatever the souls desire, extending that peaceful reception across both lives.

luna: This continuation calls the Garden a hospitality from the Forgiving and Merciful, specifying the welcome that follows the angelic reassurance in 41:30. | terra: The promised welcome is hospitality from the Forgiving, Merciful, completing the hospitable address that precedes entry into the Garden.
terra: A lifeless earth trembles and grows when watered, and its reviver will revive the dead; growing life becomes a visible analogy for afterlife.
terra: What people receive is worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for trusting believers; enduring provision lies at the destination.
terra: When wrongdoers see punishment they ask whether there is any way of return, another attempt to reverse direction only at the destination.
terra: A calamity caused by what human hands sent ahead exposes human ingratitude, showing prior action arriving as present condition.
terra: Whoever blinds himself to the Merciful's remembrance is assigned a devil as companion, tracing a present refusal of remembrance into a lasting relation.
terra: On arriving before God, that person wishes the companion were as far away as the two easts; the desired distance appears only after companionship has done its work.
terra: God's servants are addressed on that Day with no fear and no grief, the same reassuring stance as the call to the tranquil soul.
terra: The addressees are those who believed in the signs and submitted, identifying the prior response that made the peaceful address possible.
terra: “Enter the Garden” is spoken to them in joy, directly paralleling the command that concludes the settled soul's return.
terra: The Garden is said to be inherited for what its people used to do, repeating the direct passage from earlier work to lasting abode.

luna: The section cites 44:13's question about remembrance after a clear messenger; this nearby ayah has the people ask for the punishment to be removed because they believe, a concrete plea made under the crisis.

luna: The question أنى لهم الذكرى repeats the section's wording from 89:23; here a clear messenger had already come, so the shared question makes late recollection a response to rejected warning. | terra: The same question أَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ is asked after a clear messenger has already come; it makes remembrance futile because its earlier occasion was rejected.
luna: The section invokes 44:13's messenger as the reason remembrance came too late; this next ayah says they turned away from him, specifying the rejection behind that delay.

luna: After the plea in 44:12 and the messenger rejection in 44:14, this ayah says the punishment will be lifted briefly but they will return to their former course, showing how a reprieve can still be squandered.
terra: The Garden's people taste no death beyond the first death and are protected from Hell, the positive boundary opposite the state that is neither dead nor alive.
terra: Creation in truth culminates in every soul being repaid for what it earned, making embodied life accountable rather than aimless.
terra: The deniers say there is only worldly life, that people die and live, and that time destroys them; their compressed account excludes the true afterlife later encountered.
terra: They are told that they are forgotten that Day just as they forgot its meeting, making the final exclusion answer their earlier cultivated forgetfulness.
terra: Those who say “Our Lord is God” and remain upright have no fear or grief, describing the stable formation that precedes a calm return.
terra: They remain in the Garden as recompense for what they did, connecting that settled state to deeds already completed.

luna: The section's question أنى له الذكرى returns as فأنى لهم ... ذكراهم; here it is tied to the Hour arriving suddenly, making the remembrance's timing decisive. | terra: The Hour's sudden arrival is followed by فَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمْ ... ذِكْرَىٰهُمْ, exactly the section's image of recollection arriving only when its usable time has closed.
luna: After asking what remembrance will avail when the Hour comes in 47:18, this ayah commands knowledge of God and seeking forgiveness, showing the open response that precedes the late hour.
terra: The angels strike faces and backs when taking those who followed what angered God, another forced departure set against a willing return.
terra: Worldly life is play and diversion, while faith and mindfulness yield rewards without consuming people's wealth; action can be converted into lasting provision.
terra: God sends tranquility into believers' hearts so their faith increases, an indirect account of how a soul becomes settled through divine action.
terra: God knows what is in the believers' hearts, is pleased with them, sends tranquility upon them, and rewards them, joining inner settlement with divine approval.
terra: Unbelievers carry the zeal of ignorance while God sends tranquility upon His Messenger and believers, showing divine settledness overcoming an agitated moral state.

luna: The section moves from a final crisis to belated remembrance; this ayah says the agony of death brings the truth, matching the moment when reality can no longer be postponed. | terra: The stupor of death brings the truth the person had been avoiding; the previously evaded reality becomes immediate when action is ending.

luna: The section's soul faces its final encounter; this neighboring Judgment scene brings every soul with a driver and witness, specifying how the person arrives before the account. | terra: Every soul comes with a driver and a witness at judgment; the driven arrival forms a boundary around the exceptional gentleness of “return to your Lord.”

luna: The section's regret is a late awakening; this ayah says the person had been heedless and now the covering is removed, so sight becomes sharp only after the chance to act. | terra: The veil of heedlessness is removed and sight becomes sharp that Day; late clarity explains how the person can suddenly remember the life just completed.
terra: God ends the quarrel at judgment by saying that He had sent the warning ahead to them; advance warning, unlike their late dispute, arrived while response remained possible.
terra: The Garden is brought near to the mindful, placing the promised destination before the returning person without the exposure of Hell.
terra: It is promised to every أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ, one repeatedly returning and keeping faith, giving a lived form of “return to your Lord.”
terra: The entrant feared the Merciful unseen and came with قَلْبٍ مُّنِيبٍ, a heart already turned back before the meeting.
terra: ٱدْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ addresses them with peaceful entry and calls it the day of abiding, closely matching the settled soul's invitation into the Garden.
terra: Each person remains pledged for what he earned even when believing descendants are joined to their family, preserving individual moral possession within communal mercy.
terra: A human being has only what he strove for, making prior striving the actual provision later remembered or enjoyed.
terra: That striving will be seen, so effort from the hidden past becomes visible at the destination.
terra: It is then repaid with the fullest recompense, completing the movement from striving through sight to result.
terra: Everyone upon the earth passes away, stripping worldly life of any claim to permanence.
terra: The majestic, generous face of the Lord remains, supplying the enduring counterpart toward which the departing soul returns.
terra: God has apportioned death among people and cannot be forestalled, placing the end of the acting life under divine measure.
terra: God can replace people with their likes and bring them forth in a form they do not know, so departure does not limit His power to originate another life.
terra: People already know the first creation and are asked why they do not remember; remembered origin is offered before death as evidence for renewed life.
terra: The soul or life-breath reaches the throat, opening a deathbed scene closely parallel to its reaching the collarbones.
terra: Those present look on as it reaches the throat, stressing their inability to stop or reverse the departure.
terra: God is nearer to the dying person than the witnesses although they do not see, placing the hidden taking beside the visible body.
terra: The listeners are challenged, if they are truly beyond recompense, setting up return of the departing life as the test of that claim.
terra: “Bring it back” makes the breath-like return that humans cannot command explicit; only God sends a soul back from sleep or holds it at death.
terra: The deathbed passage now distinguishes the departing person who is among those brought near, beginning the peaceful outcome of the soul just taken.
terra: That person receives rest, fragrant provision, and a Garden of delight, closely paralleling the tranquil soul's welcoming destination.
terra: A second favorable case identifies the departing person as one of the companions of the right.
terra: The greeting “peace to you” follows for the companion of the right, giving a gentle reception after the soul's irretrievable departure.
terra: The departing denier who went astray begins the opposing outcome, showing why not every soul leaves in tranquility.
terra: Boiling water is that denier's first hospitality, reversing the fragrant provision of the one brought near.
terra: Burning in Hell completes the opposed reception immediately after the throat-and-return challenge.

luna: The section labels root ء ن ي as the question of whether a time has arrived; this ayah asks أَلَمْ يَأْنِ while believers still have time to humble their hearts at God's remembrance, unlike the closed moment in 89:23. | terra: The section explicitly sets أَلَمْ يَأْنِ beside late remembrance: here believers are asked whether the time has come for hearts to soften to God's remembrance while response is still possible.

luna: The section recalls how wealth is mistaken for success and then regretted; this ayah describes worldly life as adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before it withers, clarifying what passes. | terra: Worldly life is likened to admired vegetation that dries and crumbles, followed by punishment or forgiveness in the Hereafter; passing growth cannot be the lasting “my life.”
luna: After 57:20's passing worldly display, this ayah urges racing toward forgiveness and a Garden, a concrete enduring destination related to the section's recognition of the true life.
terra: Satan makes his party forget God's remembrance, tracing final loss back to an active worldly production of forgetfulness.
terra: Those supported with spirit and admitted to eternal Gardens are described by رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ, another communal form of the soul's mutual contentment.

luna: The section identifies root ق د م with good deeds sent ahead; this command asks each soul to look at ما قدمت لغد, turning the same forward-looking review into a living instruction. | terra: The command that every soul inspect مَّا قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍ turns the regret of 89:24 into a present practice: send something ahead while tomorrow is still ahead.

luna: The section ties remembrance and the soul's life to 59:18; this next ayah warns against those who forgot God and were made to forget themselves, a specific opposite to the person's belated return to what their life meant. | terra: Those who forgot God were made to forget their own souls; failed remembrance deforms the very self that must later return.
terra: The same refusal to wish for death is grounded in what their hands have sent ahead, repeating the link between advance action and fear of the meeting.

luna: The section follows the soul from its bodily life toward return and accounting; this ayah says the death one flees will meet them, then they will be returned to God and told what they did. | terra: The death people flee will meet them; afterward they return to the Knower and are informed of what they did, joining unavoidable departure, return, and recovered action.

luna: The section's root ق د م frames good work as provision sent ahead; this ayah urges spending before death and gives the same kind of last-minute plea for more time to give charity and become righteous. | terra: People are told to spend before death comes, when a soul will ask for a short delay to give charity and become righteous; present giving is something that can still be sent ahead.

luna: After the plea for delay in 63:10, this ayah says God will not postpone a soul once its term arrives, making the time boundary in the section explicit. | terra: God will not delay any soul once its term arrives, closing the very interval requested in the preceding plea.

luna: The section says people misread abundance and deprivation as honor and humiliation; this ayah calls wealth and children a trial and points to God's greater reward, giving that misreading its correction. | terra: Wealth and children are a trial while immense reward is with God, correcting the use of worldly abundance as a measure of final honor.
terra: Mary's story again uses breathed spirit and then describes her faithfulness, linking life-giving breath with a soul formed by belief and obedience.
terra: God created death and life to test who is best in deed; life is the interval for producing the action later remembered and judged.
terra: The people of the Blaze say that if they had listened or reasoned they would not be its companions; understanding arrives only inside the consequence.
terra: They confess their sin, confirming that the preceding wish is acknowledgment after the usable time for hearing has passed.
terra: The right-hand recipient openly invites others to read his book; unlike the regretful speaker, he can face the record that reached him.
terra: The recipient of the right-hand book says he knew he would meet his account; remembered accountability shaped action before the meeting rather than arising after it.
terra: He is then فِى عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ, a pleasing life that answers both “my life” and the satisfied soul's state.
terra: The pleasing life is located in a high Garden, identifying the lasting home for which the favorable record prepared.
terra: Its fruits are brought near, turning the abstract future provision into a provision now within reach.
terra: The Garden's people are told to eat and drink for بِمَآ أَسْلَفْتُمْ فِى ٱلْأَيَّامِ ٱلْخَالِيَةِ; prior deeds have actually reached the life for which 89:24 wishes it had prepared.

luna: The section's “if only” is spoken at the reckoning; here the person given the record in the left hand says يَا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُوتَ كِتَابِيَهْ, another regret after the outcome is known. | terra: The person given the book in the left hand cries يَٰلَيْتَنِى لَمْ أُوتَ كِتَٰبِيَهْ, another judgment-day wish produced by a record that can no longer be changed.

luna: Following the wish not to have received the record in 69:25, this ayah says the person did not know what their account would be, extending the same reckoning scene. | terra: He wishes he had never known his account, specifying the knowledge whose arrival now only deepens the preceding regret.

luna: The section's speaker wishes too late for a different life; this next lament wishes that death had been final, making the despair after the account explicit. | terra: He wishes the former death had been final, the inverse of recognizing the Hereafter as the true life.
terra: His wealth has not availed him, exposing the worldly possession that failed to become something sent ahead.
terra: His authority has vanished, completing the stripping away of the worldly measures by which he had understood his life.

luna: The section's stated root ق د م describes good work as provision sent ahead; this ayah says whatever good people send ahead for themselves they will find with God, completing the forward-then-arrive relation. | terra: Whatever good believers send ahead for themselves will be found with God as something better and greater in reward; the provision survives its senders.
terra: Every soul is pledged for what it earned, binding the soul's final condition to the action it sent through its worldly life.
terra: The companions of the right are excepted from the rule that every soul is pledged for its earning, marking the favorable class within that soul-and-deed formula.
terra: The warning is called a reminder, locating its purpose before the hearer reaches the threatened scene.
terra: Whoever wills may remember it, another formulation of accessible recollection during the acting life.

luna: The section explicitly names this as another state of the soul; the self-reproaching النفس contrasts with the settled soul addressed at the end of 89. | terra: The oath by the self-reproaching soul names an inner state in which wrongdoing is recognized; it can be read as a stage between the commanding self and settled tranquility.

luna: Using the section's stated root ق د م, this ayah says a person will be told what they sent ahead and left behind, spelling out the future review behind “what I sent ahead for my life.” | terra: The human being is informed on that Day of مَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ, expanding the section's one wished-for advance into a complete reckoning of what was sent ahead and left behind.
terra: People love ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ, the immediate life, naming the temporal preference that leaves no provision for later.
terra: They leave the Hereafter, completing the opposition between immediate attachment and the destination toward which the death scene soon drives them.

luna: The section's life-giving soul is shown at its bodily limit; this ayah says when it reaches the collarbones, giving a concrete death scene for the soul's departure. | terra: The life-breath reaches ٱلتَّرَاقِىَ, locating the soul's departure at the collarbones just before the final driving described later in the passage.

luna: The death scene invoked by the section continues with the question مَنْ رَاقٍ, “who can cure?”, as those present confront the soul's failing body. | terra: The bystanders ask who can provide a cure or incantation, giving the human side of the deathbed scene after the soul reaches the collarbones.

luna: Continuing the death scene connected to the section's soul, this ayah says the dying person realizes it is separation, naming what the body is undergoing. | terra: The dying person realizes أَنَّهُ ٱلْفِرَاقُ, naming the separation that the section imagines through breath leaving the body.

luna: The section describes the soul's departure; this next ayah depicts the legs drawn together in the final bodily moment before the return named in 75:30. | terra: One leg is wound around the other, adding the body's final helplessness before the soul's movement toward its Lord.

luna: The section says the tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord; this ayah says إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمَسَاقُ, while in the death scene the soul is driven to its Lord. | terra: إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ ٱلْمَسَاقُ says the final driving is to the Lord; the section explicitly sets this compelled movement against the settled soul's addressed return.
terra: The human is asked whether he thinks he will be left without purpose, challenging life understood without test or return.
terra: The Creator of the human stages is surely able to revive the dead, answering the aimlessness challenged earlier in the passage.
terra: A span of time passed over the human when he was not a thing مَّذْكُورًا; the remembrance root here means being mentioned and frames human life within time before conscious memory.
terra: Humanity is created from a mixed drop as a test and given hearing and sight, specifying the embodied, responsible life that follows the unmentioned state.
terra: Garden dwellers are told that their reward is theirs and their striving has been appreciated; the later address confirms that their earlier effort arrived.
terra: People love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy Day, treating the coming reality as if it could remain behind them.

luna: The section's root ق د م links to ما قدمت يداه, but here the review ends in the disbeliever's wish to be dust; the verse makes the section's late regret concrete. | terra: On the near Day, a person sees مَا قَدَّمَتْ يَدَاهُ and the unbeliever wishes to be dust; sight of what the hands sent ahead produces the same too-late wish.

luna: The section says the remembrance scene in 79:35 begins with الطامة الكبرى; this is that overwhelming calamity, the event that makes the following recollection belated. | terra: This ayah brings ٱلطَّآمَّةُ ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ; it opens the judgment scene whose next ayah supplies the belated remembrance.

luna: The section's stated root ذ ك ر and its sense of pursuing what is gone meet يَتَذَكَّرُ here: on the day of the great calamity, a person recalls ما سعى, what they strove for. | terra: At the great catastrophe, the human being remembers مَا سَعَىٰ, directly matching the section's person who remembers past striving when Hell is brought into view.

luna: The section connects 79:35's belated recollection to the great calamity; this next ayah says Hell is exposed for whoever sees, completing the Judgment scene that provokes the memory. | terra: Hell is exposed لِمَن يَرَىٰ immediately after the person's remembrance, completing the same sight-and-recollection sequence as 89:23.
luna: The section links the Day of account to the soul's final state; this adjoining passage introduces the one who transgressed before 79:38 names the preference that determines the contrast.

luna: The section's “my life” is finally understood as the lasting one; this ayah identifies the opposing choice as preferring الحياة الدنيا. | terra: The transgressor preferred worldly life, giving the choice that precedes the exposed Hell and belated recollection in this same passage.

luna: After the person who prefers worldly life in 79:38, this ayah names Hell as the refuge, making the consequence of that choice explicit. | terra: Hell is the refuge of the one who preferred worldly life, connecting that preference to the scene in which Hell becomes visible.

luna: The section's closing soul is calm and welcomed; this counterpart describes one who feared standing before the Lord and restrained the soul from desire. | terra: The one who fears standing before the Lord restrains ٱلنَّفْسَ from desire; the self is disciplined before judgment instead of regretting after it.

luna: The section's final soul is invited toward its Lord; this next ayah gives the corresponding refuge for the restrained soul as the Garden. | terra: The Garden is that person's refuge, completing the alternative to both exposed Hell and the wish that nothing had been sent ahead.
terra: The revelation is itself a reminder, presenting remembrance in an available form before it becomes a recovered past.
terra: Whoever wills may remember it, describing the open agency that contrasts with remembrance after judgment has arrived.
luna: The section's late review of a person's life is staged in a Judgment sequence; this ayah says the records are opened before Hell is kindled and every soul knows what it brought.
luna: The section's scene begins when Hell is brought forth and a person remembers too late; this neighboring passage says الجحيم is kindled before the next ayah says each soul knows what it brought.
luna: The section's late accounting scene is paired here with الجنة أزلفت, the Garden brought near; the next ayah completes the scene by saying each soul knows what it brought.

luna: The section's human remembers only when the end arrives; this ayah says علمت نفس ما أحضرت, that each soul knows what it has brought, in the same Judgment sequence as Hell and the Garden. | terra: When the cosmic veils are removed, every soul knows مَّآ أَحْضَرَتْ, what it has brought with it; deeds are present at the destination reached by the soul.

luna: The section labels root ن ف س through the dictionary form التنفس, air leaving the inside; the Qur'an's يَتَنَفَّسَ describes dawn as breathing, a direct image built from that secondary sense. | terra: The dawn is sworn by إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ, “when it breathes”; this is the Qur'anic breathing image that makes visible the dictionary source's outward movement of نَفَس.
luna: The section centers a soul's final awareness; this adjacent Judgment scene has the graves scattered before 82:5 says each soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind.

luna: The section's root ق د م names deeds sent forward; here every soul learns what it قدمت وأخرت, so the verse makes the same accounting apply to each person. | terra: عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ مَّا قَدَّمَتْ وَأَخَّرَ joins the section's two key terms, soul and sending ahead, at the moment when the world's order breaks open.
terra: On that Day no soul controls anything for another soul and command belongs to God, isolating each returning soul with its fixed record.
terra: Humanity is addressed as laboring toward its Lord and destined to meet Him; every present exertion is already traveling to the encounter.
terra: The person given the record in the right hand begins the favorable version of that meeting.
terra: He receives an easy accounting, the outcome of deeds prepared before the meeting rather than a late wish.
terra: He returns joyfully to his people, a peaceful return that echoes the settled soul's contented return.
terra: The one given the record behind his back begins the opposite return scene.
terra: He calls for destruction, another judgment-day utterance whose wish cannot change the record.
terra: He enters a Blaze, giving the consequence that prompts the preceding cry.

luna: The section says people mistake worldly ease for honor and realize the truth too late; this ayah describes a person who had been joyful among his family before the reckoning. | terra: He had been joyful among his people, showing a worldly contentment whose object and duration differed from the joyful return in 84:9.

luna: The family ease in 84:13 is followed by the person's belief that he would never return; this supplies the mistaken view of the afterlife that the section's late regret overturns. | terra: He thought he would never return, exposing the false belief beneath his former ease.

luna: This reply to the person who thought he would not return says his Lord had always seen him, completing the passage's correction of that false security. | terra: His Lord was always seeing him, correcting the denied return with the continuous divine knowledge that grounds his account.
terra: The command فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ asks for reminder while it can benefit, the live side of 89:23's question about a reminder that can no longer do so.
terra: The one who fears receives the reminder, identifying the responsive hearer before the passage turns to the person who avoids it.
terra: The most wretched person avoids the reminder, supplying the earlier refusal that makes later recognition in the Fire useless.
terra: That person enters the great Fire; it gives the destination reached after refusing the reminder in the preceding ayah.
terra: In that Fire the person neither dies nor lives, a stark boundary around “life” that clarifies why the Hereafter can be encountered without becoming the wished-for life.
terra: Success belongs to one who purifies the self, showing a path from the commanding or reproaching self toward the settled soul.
terra: The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and prays; remembrance here becomes action sent ahead rather than a thought recovered too late.

luna: The section says the dying person finally places “my life” in the right horizon; this ayah names the error as preferring الحياة الدنيا over the lasting life. | terra: Preferring ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا identifies the mistaken placement of “my life” that 89:24 corrects only after judgment.

luna: Completing 87:16's contrast, this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more enduring, supporting the section's claim that true life is beyond the present one. | terra: The Hereafter is better and more lasting, stating why deeds must be prepared for that life rather than for the preferred nearer one.
terra: Faces are joyful on that Day, beginning the opposite outcome to the face and voice of belated regret.
terra: Those faces are لِّسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ, satisfied with their prior striving; 79:35's remembered striving has here become a source of contentment.
terra: They are in a high Garden, giving the destination of the satisfied striving named immediately before it.

luna: The section's addressed soul is settled; this ayah also names the النفس but describes its formation, beginning a passage that distinguishes its corrupt and purified outcomes. | terra: The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it treats the soul as something formed for a moral history, not merely an escaping breath.

luna: The section contrasts a tranquil soul with souls in turmoil; this continuation says the soul is inspired with its wickedness and piety, the two possibilities behind that contrast. | terra: The soul is inspired with its wickedness and mindfulness, naming the opposing possibilities behind the commanding, reproaching, and settled states.

luna: The section's final soul is welcomed; this ayah says the one who purifies the soul succeeds, giving the positive counterpart to the soul states named in the section. | terra: Success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, describing the transformation whose settled result can return contentedly.

luna: Completing 91:9's contrast, this ayah says the one who corrupts the soul fails, a contrary outcome to the section's tranquil soul. | terra: Failure belongs to the one who buries or corrupts the soul, the opposing formation that ends in belated recognition.
terra: The most mindful gives wealth to purify himself, making purification an outward deed sent toward the lasting outcome.
terra: His giving seeks only the face of his Lord Most High, fixing the true destination of what he sends ahead.
terra: وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ promises that he will be satisfied, a future contentment produced by God-directed preparation.
terra: The Lord promises to give until the addressee is satisfied, a prophetic instance of future contentment grounded in divine giving.
terra: The return is to the Lord, a compact statement of the direction spoken more gently to the tranquil soul.
terra: Eternal Gardens culminate in رَّضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ, the mutual satisfaction unfolded in the address to the satisfied, approved soul.

luna: The section's person remembers what they did at Judgment; here people emerge أشتاتا ليروا أعمالهم, in groups to see their deeds, making the review public and concrete. | terra: People issue forth separately to be shown their deeds, beginning a judgment scene in which nothing sent ahead remains hidden.

luna: The section's regret concerns what was or was not sent ahead; this next ayah specifies that even an atom's weight of good is seen, giving the review in 99:6 its smallest scale. | terra: Whoever did an atom's weight of good sees it, making the smallest prior provision present in the later life.

luna: As a continuation of the deed-review scene related to the section's late awareness, this ayah says even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the two-sided accounting. | terra: Whoever did an atom's weight of evil sees it, completing the exactness of that recovered past.
terra: Heavy scales identify the person whose earlier deeds have weight at judgment, the fulfilled counterpart to wishing one had prepared.
terra: That person is فِى عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ, another direct joining of true life with satisfaction.
terra: Competitive accumulation distracts people, naming the worldly absorption that keeps them from preparing for their real life.
terra: The distraction continues until they visit the graves, setting death as the point at which its hold is finally exposed.
terra: “You will soon know” warns of knowledge arriving after the distraction, akin to recollection at the revealed consequence.
terra: The warning “again, you will soon know” intensifies the staged arrival of certainty beyond the grave.
terra: The condemned person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, embodying investment in what cannot become lasting provision.
terra: He thinks his wealth has made him immortal, attaching life to possession in the precise way judgment will overturn.
